messages.subject: How to eliminate unwanted line breaks
messages.subject_clean: How to eliminate unwanted line breaks
messages.body_plain:
Hello R enthusiasts.

I have some hand-me-down corpus files that have unwanted line breaks
in the middle of sentences. I used the function paste(file, collapse="
") to eliminate those line breaks and put line-final words next to
line-initial words, in preparation for retrieving bigrams. However,
when I use the function strsplit(file, sep="[.,?!]") to break up the
single-element vector (which has 700,000 words), it never finishes
working, at least not after seven hours, when I stopped it.

I discovered the following warning about strsplit() in the manual:
"The standard regular expression code has been reported to be very
slow when applied to extremely long character strings (tens of
thousands of characters or more): the code used when perl = TRUE seems
much faster and more reliable for such usages." With a corpus file of
700,000 words, it was little wonder why it never finished the
operation.

Does anyone have any words of wisdom on how to put line-final words
back together with line-initial words in preparation for retrieving
bigrams in a file with 700,000 words?

Thanks. Earl Brown

messages.body_plain:
> What happens when [...]
I am not sure what you mean by "What happens when [...]" but a rather
inelegant solution to this problem is this (again using the Brown
corpus, which is 40% larger than your corpus:

###########################
# load Brown corpus tagged, strip tags, strip line numbers
x.1 <- scan("/home/stgries/Corpora/ICAME2/BROWN_tagged_brownscheme/BTL.TXT",

what=character(0), sep="\n", quote="", comment.char="")

x.1 <- gsub("_[^ ]+", "", x.1, perl=T)
x.1 <- sub("^.*? ", "", x.1, perl=T)

# take time
date()

x.2 <- gsub("([\\.\\?\\!\\:])", "\\1\n", x.1, perl=TRUE) # look for
punctuation marks
x.3 <- paste(x.2, collapse=" ") # collapse with line break
output.file <- "temp.txt" # define temporary output file
cat(x.3, file=output.file, sep="") # print corpus into temp. file with
no sep character
x.4 <- scan(output.file, what=character(0), sep="\n", quote="",
comment.char="") # loade it again from there; result: vector of
'sentences'

bigrams <- character() # define bigram collector
# loop through each 'sentence' and get word bigrams
for (each.sentence in x.4) {
   bigrams <- append(bigrams, word.grammy(each.sentence, 2)) #
word.grammy != regular R function, you will need your own there
}

# take time again
date()
###########################

Takes 45 sec between the first and the second "date()" on this machine:

Processor: 3x AMD Phenom(tm) 8450 Triple-Core Processor
Memory: 2797MB
Operating System: Ubuntu 9.04

HTH,

STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

messages.subject: Model checking
messages.body_plain:
# sorry for double posting

Hi everybody
,
I was wondering if anyone has come across a decent description of the
model checking process in R.

I am trying to fit a Poisson Generalized Linear Model for Count Data
and am still rather inexperienced with these things (and I guess GLMs
in general). When asked to plot a given model, R outputs a series of
four graphs (residuals x fitted, QQ, ...). Now, I find these plots
rather hard to interpret. The most thorough discussion I know of how
these things should look like is Crawley 2007 (The R book), but the
comments there are a little "impressionistic" at times ("This plot
should look like a sky at night” Crawley 2007:357;  "[nonconstancy of
variance] shows up as a triangular scatter (like a wedge of cheese)”
Crawley 2007:359...).

To put it bluntly: I am having trouble deciding if what I see is
sufficiently similar to a sky at night or a wedge of cheese...;) Any
hint as to where I can find a model answer for (Poisson Generalized
Linear) Model checking and the interpretation of those plots would be
tremendously appreciated.

best,
daniel

- require as input a vector of words, and
- return all consecutive y-grams,

i.e., something that would work like this:

word.grammy(c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"), 2)

I guess this is not difficult to put into a function, a few lines
should do the job.

Cheers,

STG

messages.body_plain:
I used to work in text retrieval (what y'all call search engines now).
I'm not convinced that such a specific task is suited to either
Microsoft's offering or to R. Especially since you make no mention of
data volume other than there being a very large drive. How many
documents/year? How many words per document? Is this a one off
requirement or a regular task? Are you only looking to find which
files contain the word (why not a phrase)?

You might to better to look at using Apache's Lucene text retrieval
system or a derivative of it. But without more data on the data
there's nothing else to recommend.

messages.body_plain:
Bob,

In that case and assuming that the only analsysis is the *presence* of
these words, synonms or collocates then I'd go with Lucene. Check out
http://lucene.apache.org/ for details. There are input modules to deal
with both Microsoft Word formats and with PDF. But yo'll have to dig
for them. Keep the Lucene index files around and later searches will
be quicker as it won't have to rescan the old texts. I don't recall
the details but it's something like O(n log(n)) for a Lucene search,
where n is the number of documents to be scanned/searched. (A grep
solution is O(n).)

Of course if you're going to do *any* analysis of the texts then you
will have to look at R and also probabaly the tm text mining package,
The paper in the Journal of Statistical Software at
http://www.jstatsoft.org/v25/i05 describes that package's
capabilities. Supposed to cope with both Word and PDF encoded
documents; my personal use is only with plain text files. You may be
able to manipulate your "large disk of documents" as a repository
within tm, though we might well refer to these repositories as
corpora.

And of course, Lucene, R and the tm package have the benefit of
zero-cost licenses.

messages.subject: Testing how "unnormal" some data might be.
messages.subject_clean: Testing how "unnormal" some data might be.
messages.body_plain:
Hello Group,

I've been searching the web for an answer to this question but have
yet to find one.

What I am currently doing.

The following produces a density plot of the numeric data and overlays
a normal curve. The normal curve is derived from the numeric data's
mean, standard deviation, min and max values. This creates a graph
that is easy to visually evaluate how skewed or un-normal the density
of the data being analyzed is.

object1 <- c(1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7,7,7, 8, 9, 9, 10)
#not real data, the real set is 500+ numbers
object1.d <- density(object1)
plot(object1.d)
plot(function(x)dnorm(x,mean=mean(object1),sd=sd(object1)), max
(object1.d$x),min(object1.d$x), add=TRUE, lty=1,lwd=3)

where object1 is a numeric variable.

What I'm trying to do.

I would like a more robust / valid method with which to determine how
close to normal my data's density plot is. Essentially I would like to
compare the generated value to the actual value and determine if the
difference between the two is significant or past some thresh hold.
Another approach would be just to see how normal my data is, but I am
unsure of how to do that as well. This was the best approach I could
come up with at the moment.

What I tried.
